utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom because the Chamber understands that there are no preliminary matters to be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vracar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Vracar. Mr. Vracar, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vracar. For the record, could you please slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: My name is Nikola Vracar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D1721 on our screens, please. I don't know about the rest of the courtroom, but we do not have this document on our screens. Oh, okay, now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vracar, you see the document on the left.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this last page, do you see a signature and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this statement accurately reflect what you said to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you said to us and what is recorded in this statement, is that accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give me the same answers, in principle?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1721 receives number D789, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was no associated exhibits since all the exhibits mentioned in the statement are already in the evidence. With your leave, Your Honours, I would just read statement summary of Mr. Vracar and then I would have several questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As a reserve police officer in Kljuc, Nikola Vracar witnessed the interethnic breakdown, both at the police and the society as a whole. On 27th of May, 1992, Mr. Vracar was wounded when the illegally armed Muslim forces murdered Dusko Stojakovic, the deputy commander of the Kljuc public security station. On that same day, he saw armed Muslim formations at Pudin Han immediately before the ambush and murder of six unarmed young soldiers who were travelling home to Serbia from Knin, having completed their mandatory military service. He knows about the blowing up of the Banja Luka radio and TV signal repeater at the village of Ramici which happened on the same day. That was the beginning of the war in Kljuc. Before the above events, not a single non-Serb in Kljuc was hurt or murdered. He heard about the incident at Velagici as he was still on sick-leave at that time. He has information that proceedings were instituted against the perpetrators. As a member of the police, he took part in the apprehension of individuals who committed criminal offence, which is how the entire police force acted. The police work conditions were aggravated during the night, as there was no power and water in the city. All inhabitants were affected by the lack of fuel, flour, and medications. Nikola Vracar will provide information as to which villages saw no combat actions and why, and testify that the army was mostly outside Kljuc, as the city was not in the zone of combat activities. He claims that the movement of Serb and non-Serb inhabitants out of the area was caused by the fear of war and that it was voluntarily. That was the statement summary, and I would have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We need D789 on our screens. That is the statement of the witness. We need page 3 in both versions. Actually, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vracar, you see paragraph 12 of your statement before you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what you said there. You said that you somehow managed to report via radio that you had been attacked and wounded. When was it that you managed that and what kind of equipment did you use?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: After combat, I withdrew into a forest and after about an hour, a bit more than an hour, I went to the village of Ramici and on the road I encountered a police vehicle, and then I said that they should communicate via their own equipment that we had been attacked, that the late Stojakovic was killed, that Kecman and Bajic had been wounded and that I didn't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us move on to the next page in both versions. We need paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the second sentence here, you say that the Muslim forces chose those days for attacking the Serb forces. When you say "Serb forces," what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The police only. Because there was no army there. The TO units had exercises at Cadjevica, in the area of Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we need page 7 and paragraph 35 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vracar, in this paragraph, you speak of the killings of Muslims at the school in Velagici. You said that you had only heard about that. You also said what you knew as to who had committed the killing, or killings. Who arrested these Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, before the arrest, there was a check-point on the road between Velagici and Sanica. On the same day, the 27th of May when we were attacked in Krasulje, that is to say, our patrol, the check-point was attacked as well. Afterwards, the check-point was disbanded and the police carried out arrests of persons that they thought should be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we need paragraph 36. In that paragraph, you say that everybody was saying that 1941 was being repeated, and you say: "People talked that the same Muslims were attacking the Serbs, just as it had happened at the beginning of World War II in these areas." In order to have a better picture, could you please tell us how many Serbs were killed in Ribnik that you hail from during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: In the Second World War -- well, Ribnik is an ethnically pure village and it had terrible casualties. 1.300 civilians were killed. Many soldiers were killed during the war too but that is not the topic of this conversation. So many people no longer had any male children. Entire families were wiped out. It so happened that up until the 1960s there were certain families that had no military conscripts to send to do their service in the army because there simply were no boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During this war, this last war in Bosnia, from 1992 to 1995, did you lose any members of your own family during the breakthrough of the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I can say that there were several victims in my family. First, two elderly relatives Dara and Mladjen Vracar, they were 80 years old or even older. They were killed, I don't know how. My aunt was burned alive, and my uncle, her husband, was killed. After the Dayton Accords, we found the mortal remains of my aunt and uncle, and we buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us briefly go back to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment at page 6, line 24, the transcript reads, "I don't know." I think I heard, but I stand corrected when I'm wrong, "I don't know how." And usually I'm not dealing with these kind of matters because it will be done overnight but here it could lead to some misunderstanding. Please proceed. Is that what you said, that you didn't know how your two elderly relatives were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's just that we have your answer correctly on the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judge just helped us so that the transcript could be corrected. So, once again, paragraph 35, where the killings in Velagici are mentioned. What was it that you heard? Who were the perpetrators of these killings?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: After the 27th of May, I was undergoing medical treatment and since Kljuc is a small place, people talked and everybody knows everything. People were saying that these were some kind of paramilitary units that had come and committed that crime. I don't know who they were. Later on, there was also talk about them being captured, prosecuted, and so on, but, again, I don't know whether that actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there things that people said in relation to the Second World War and these killings?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, yes. Rumour had it that somebody had done this out of revenge because their own families had fallen victim during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vracar. That is all that we had for you at this point in time. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before we'll start with the cross-examination by the Prosecution, I'd like to ask two, perhaps three additional questions in relation to your statement. In paragraph 17 of your statement, you say: "It is important to note that during the above combat action by the Muslim army, the TO battalion of the legitimate municipality of Kljuc was not in the town of Kljuc, but ... training on Manjaca ..." Could you tell us what you exactly mean by "legitimate municipality of Kljuc"? Was there a legitimate one and an illegitimate one? And what made one legitimate and the other not legitimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to say that after the multi-party elections there was a political rift in the municipal leadership, and the SDA Assemblymen proclaimed the Muslim municipality of Kljuc. However, according to the constitution that was in force then, the municipality had its Territorial Defence and they sent them out for military training for an exercise in Cadjevica in the Manjaca area. I meant the Territorial Defence that had remained under the legal organs of government. Because these people from the SDA, they declared this independent municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. One other question. In paragraph 23, you say: "A decision was made at the level of the municipality of Kljuc that anyone who wished to leave had to surrender his property and get the necessary confirmations." Why did someone wanted to leave, surrender his property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, property had to be handed over so that it could be recorded and made available to Serb refugees so that there would be no looting of property. At the beginning of the war, during this chaos, there were a lot of looters, bandits, who stole people's property, and that's why all of this was written up. People received certificates to that effect for another reason too. Once they return, after the war, they would be entitled to this property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was the decision made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember the exact date but it was sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that before the 17th, when you said the -- I think you said it was the 17th that -- was it before the 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I was not employed in the administration, nor was I in any organs of authority or government organs, so I don't know. But I know that this is what was said, that this was the procedure for the people who wanted to move out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that applied to all people who would move out, even if only temporarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it applied to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's the first time in this case that you're examining a witness. Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, you'll now cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You find her to your right. Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vracar.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you can hear me in a language you understand; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. To start your cross-examination, I just want to begin by getting you to confirm, you've actually come to this Tribunal before, haven't you? You testified as a Defence witness in the case of Mr. Brdjanin in 2003; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So I'd like to actually go back to some of the evidence you gave in that case for us to start out. I want to get you to confirm some of the evidence you previously gave. So maybe just to begin, you can confirm, can't you, that -- your previous evidence that you were mobilised in April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, you can also confirm that you were a reserve policeman even before April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 6 of your written evidence, you said, "I performed police tasks," to describe your duties. And, in fact, you -- your police tasks were that you were a member of the intervention unit for the Kljuc SJB; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as a member of the intervention unit, you got some specialised training in Manjaca at the training grounds there; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I have to say at this point that this was general infantry training. It wasn't any kind of special training. It was just infantry training, like any other armed unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So that training included training in the use of mortars; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That depended. I wasn't involved in that, but there were some squads who had training on mortars, but I was just a shooter, an infantryman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now, here I'd actually like to just show you what you told the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case, and maybe that's going to help you refresh your memory, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 65 ter number 31602. And it's going to be in English, unfortunately, but I'll read it to you. 31602; e-court page 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, here is a transcript of -- actually, if we could go over and start at 32, please. It's -- it's the transcript of your testimony in the Brdjanin case. And at the very bottom of the page, my former colleague, Mrs. Korner, asks you: "And the training that you received in Manjaca was training in the," and then if we could go to the second page, "in the uses of mortars. That's right isn't it?" And you said, "Yes it is." And then -- I'll just go on. She asked, "Zoljas?" And you replied, "Yes." She asked, "Heavy machine-guns?" And you confirmed, "Yes." And then she asked, "Hand-to hand combat?" And you confirmed, "Yes." And also added that you excelled at that because you're a karate expert. That -- that evidence is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now this training that you received was conducted not only by instructors from the police centre in Banja Luka but you also had instructors from the army; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as a member of the intervention unit, your direct supervisor was Vinko Kondic; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he was the SJB commander, the chief of police, for Kljuc municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the hierarchy within the police, it's correct, isn't it, that the public security station in Kljuc was exclusively linked to the Banja Luka CSB; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The CSB in Prijedor. Because the police was organised that way. There were two centres: Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'm a little puzzled by that and I'll show you why. If we could have a look at D358, please. It's a document that was prepared and signed by your boss, Vinko Kondic. And it's information on the activities of the Kljuc SJB from July 1992. You see the first page of it there. And if we could go in the English translation to the first paragraph under section 3, and in your language to page 5, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the page number for the English version?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: English version, page 3, paragraph -- first section under paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, here's your boss saying in the second sentence under section III: "After the MUP in the former BH fell apart completely, the SJB's work was exclusively linked to the Banja Luka security service centre from the start. The SJB kept the competent organs of the Serbian municipality of Kljuc informed about its work on a regular basis." So you're not saying your boss got it wrong, are you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, listen, for -- on several occasions they reorganised things, so this is probably correct, because he can't say things that are not consistent. But up there it says the centre of security services. In other words, all these centres were under the chapeau Banja Luka. That was the police. Now, what transpired during these various reorganisations, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to go to another document before we sort of leave the area of the police and its operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 65 ter 31605.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a document you were shown during your Brdjanin testimony. Otherwise possibly duplicated at 15055. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, wrong document. Could we have 15055, please. Oh, and, Your Honour, I apologise, my first time back in some time, I may have transposed the odd number and I will do my utmost to be careful about this. It was -- I have a bit of a reputation that way, and I always endeavour to have somebody else check my numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, for the first day, we're very lenient, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 65 ter 15055 is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's okay then. Thank you. We'll be able to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually want to go to the day of the 27th of May that my colleague Mr. Lukic discussed with you, and according to your evidence at paragraph 8, it looks like there were only eight people on the scene. And if you want to, I have a look -- I've got your statement here and you can have a look at paragraph 8. But, actually, the police vehicle that was on the scene with you, that you spoke about in your statement, didn't hold only the four people that you named. It was a kombi van that was containing seven or eight other people; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we D789 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two vehicles: There was a van and a Golf vehicle. There were four of us in the Golf and as for the van, there were eight people. However, there were actually nine people. That's what I learned later on. I thought there were eight of them but that's not correct. There were nine of them. So in total, there were 13 men in the patrol.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now my colleague Mr. Lukic said that Mr. Stojanovic [sic] was murdered. He was actually killed as a result of the gun battle in the ambush; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton is it "Stojanovic" or "Stojakovic"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard you say indeed say "Stojanovic," but the transcript reads "Stojakovic," which makes me feel better at ease, yes. Mr. Stojanovic is still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Mr. Stojakovic was killed in the gun battle that followed the ambush; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, listen, I have to explain this. He was killed because we ran into an ambush and we didn't get out of the car. Now -- we got out of the vehicle but because he was a heavy-set man, he had difficulty. He was slow in getting out. So as he was trying to get out, he was mowed down by machine-gun fire. He wasn't killed in fighting. He was killed without any combat. He wasn't in combat. Do you understand? It's one thing when a person is killed in combat and another when they're just murdered. You understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Now, in fact, in fact, you were all armed, and you said that in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to be more specific, you all had pistols and you all had automatic rifles; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also had grenades; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, some of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, your evidence in the Brdjanin case was not that nobody fired back. Your evidence in the Brdjanin case as to how things transpired was exactly the opposite. You got out of the car. He was killed because he couldn't move fast enough. But you all fired back; right? It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. That's when the fighting began. They opened fire on us, and then we had to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the wound - because that's how you described the injury you received that day - it would kind of -- just left like it was -- make us think that you were also shot but, in fact, your evidence in the Brdjanin case was that you jumped down a slope just below the road and you hit a rock there and you dislocated your shoulder; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that injury actually didn't prevent you from at one point throwing one of those grenades that you were armed with; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, madam, but I threw those grenades before and then as I was moving backwards, I fell from a rock and my shoulder was dislocated totally, my right shoulder. You can't really fling grenades if your arm is totally dislocated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 12. Oh, we have it on the screen, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This emergency vehicle that came along and helped you, there was a doctor in the vehicle, right, Emir Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your boss also came along, Mr. Kondic; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. He and Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Emir Kapetanovic is a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing questionable there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he was arrested by the police and later taken to Manjaca. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Now, just if we could go over to paragraph 15 in both languages, your statement. That story you recount in paragraph 15 about the attack on the military bus is something you didn't personally see at all; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see it. But while I was in hospital --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: -- three dead soldiers and some wounded were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Vracar --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's -- I know you're here to tell your experiences and observations, but my question called for a pretty simple answer. Thank you. And the information that you give us in paragraph 16, about the attack on the repeater, that's also something that you didn't personally see at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's correct, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, for a dislocated shoulder, you went back to work a whole month later, on 28 June, 1992; right? Vidovdan?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were a duty officer in the op's room. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Junior duty officer or assistant duty officer, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was at -- in the op's room at the Kljuc police station; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with Your Honours' leave I just want to change topics and move on, thank you, to another area. Now I just want to talk, Mr. Vracar, about the killings in Velagici that you've spoken of in paragraph 35 of your evidence. Now, just to be perfectly clear, the information you have is only rumours, the talk of the town; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That was what people were saying. Kljuc is a small town, and people were talking about this. It was a horrible incident for a place that small, so people talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the horrible incident that we're talking about is the killing of at least 77 men who were detained in the school house in Velagici; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I don't know how many people there were there. Somebody should know. And that is who should be prosecuted, the perpetrator, and they must know about this. Now, all I know is what people said about it, citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you agree it happened, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, yes. That happened. Everyone knows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well -- but -- but you -- I suppose you don't know that the perpetrators, the people you say everyone was describing as paramilitaries, actually identified themselves in a letter to General Talic, the 1 KK commander, just two days after the killing. And in that letter, they all confirmed that they were members of the Bosnian Serb army. You didn't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, this is the first time that I hear that. I was on medical leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, for the record, that's P3528, pages 38 to 40, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ... go on to the other incident that you spoke about in your evidence, and that's the killings at Biljani and you talked about that in paragraph 37 of your statement. It's on the screen in front of us in English. If we could go over it that paragraph in B/C/S. And, there, you say: "I didn't know anything about the killings at Biljani during the war. I found about the incident afterwards, when I testified in the Brdjanin case." So, now, here again, we're talking about the killing of at least 144 males who had been detained in the school house in Biljani; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where they were detained, believe me. They were detained somewhere, but where exactly, I don't know. This town is about 16 kilometres north-west of Kljuc. And I was in a totally different area. I was being treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you're not disagreeing that it -- you're not saying that it didn't happen, are you? You agree that this happened.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, it happened. Of course it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at document P2064.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's an Official Note from the SJB in Kljuc relating to the mopping up action in Sanica on the 10th of July, 1992. It's a document, Mr. Vracar, relating to this incident. And you were actually shown this document during your testimony in the Brdjanin case as well. And if you could go down to about halfway through that large paragraph, you see that the commander of the Sanica station says: "It was planned to put the military prisoners in the area school in Biljani. For these requirements, I received help from the section for intervention of the mobile unit of the Kljuc SJB." That's precisely your unit; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That was the units I was a member of.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So who went? Who went, Mr. Vracar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. Somebody must have put together a list of people who were supposed to go there, probably the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's a bit surprising, Mr. Vracar, because your previous evidence in the Brdjanin case was that you were at work the very next day after this incident and you heard about it almost immediately. And you're telling us now you don't know who, from your unit, went on scene?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, the police station had about 300 to 400 men at the time, to be honest with you. I didn't know what the schedules were. The police commander would actually sign off on a shift list, and whom he sent, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, the intervention unit was a small unit of specialised officers. You were a member, and you were at work the very day after the incident as an assistant duty officer. And your evidence today is that you didn't know -- you don't know who went?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, believe me, there were a lot of police there. In Sanica there was a squad of police, a police squad, I don't know how many men. I also don't know how many men from Kljuc went there, or who. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could I just intervene for one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was put to you that you testified in the Brdjanin case that you learned about the incident, apart from details and who went there, the day after it happened. Is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I knew about it on the same day. I mean, the second or third day after it. There were men there. There was fighting and so on. I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that a lot of people were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That those were people that had been detained at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if they were detained. So somebody brought them there, detained them. What they did, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you learned about a larger number of people being killed at Biljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your statement, to which you attested this morning, says: "I found out about this incident afterwards when I testified in the Brdjanin case ..." What you're telling us now contradicts what is in your statement and is in line apparently with what you testified in the Brdjanin case. Any comment to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what, Mr. President? I testified 13 years ago. Human memory is not all that certain. People forget. I cannot remember all the details of things that happened 13 years ago or 20 or 22 years ago. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not talking about details. We're talking about when you learned for the first time about the incident in Biljani. That's not a detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a day or two after that happened, a day or two later. I don't know whether it was the first or the second day after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do we not find that in your statement? Why is it now, where apparently your memory serves you sufficiently to remember what you remembered at the time you gave to Brdjanin testimony, what makes it that you -- that we do not find that information in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you signed that statement? It was quite a while after you had been interviewed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean you signed it a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I gave the statement -- you mean the Brdjanin case? Or this last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This last one I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was in January last year and in July this year. January, July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, were you interviewed twice in -- before July, or were you interviewed once before July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twice, twice. I think once in January and once in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not interviewed a year before on the 23rd of January, 2013? That would be close to two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- when were you, for the first time, interviewed by the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this year, that is, approximately a year ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now was it this year or last year? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2013 or 2014, not sure. But it was January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not interviewed in January 2013 and in January 2014 with a year interval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No. Just one January, one July. The year I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that in January? Were you interviewed for one day or for -- on several days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One day. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one day. Now, you signed your statement in July. Were you interviewed again in July, or did you just come to sign your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you not, at that time, carefully read the statement so that you would find out that there is apparently a mistake in when you learned about the Biljani incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I didn't pay attention to such details. I thought that everything was okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not carefully and thoroughly read through your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I read the statement, but I didn't pay attention to that detail. One sentence, when I did this or that. It's a detail, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You consider it still not to be very important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly it's an oversight on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton -- well, I say please proceed, but we'd rather take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge would have one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were member of an intervention unit. How many people were members of this intervention unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. The unit consisted of three platoons; that's to say, about a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And your platoon, how many people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the break, I have one additional question. Were all these three platoons men from Kljuc or was it just your platoon or -- could you tell us how many Kljuc members there were in this intervention unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the people were from our municipality, the municipality of Kljuc. That is to say, all members of the reserve police, or, rather, the milicija, came from the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means all hundred in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately three platoons of 100 men, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We take a break. We take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I use the time for the following: Perhaps I should address you, Mr. Tieger. The Defence has filed a motion yesterday for an extension of time for the deadline to respond to the Prosecution's 45th 92 bis motion. The Defence seeks 30 days extra. Has the Prosecution already taken a position on that? I think when you asked for the re-opening of your case that you said that you would have a reasonable request for further time. Would -- would not find any opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, I see no reason why we wouldn't abide by our customary approach and not oppose, but if you'll give me until the end of this session to confirm that there's nothing special about the circumstance that warrants a change, I will confirm that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we hear from you later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, from body language, I understood that the missing document in e-court had been uploaded meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, I would just like to stay on the subject of the massacres at Biljani for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vracar, in your Brdjanin testimony -- and we could pull it up on the screen for the gentleman. It's 65 ter 31602. And I think probably e-court page 49, if I'm not mistaken. Your indulgence for just a moment. If you could scroll down the page. I omitted to write the e-court page number. And go to the next page, please, page 50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Vracar, what your testimony was in the Brdjanin case is on the screen here in front of you. I'm going to read it to you and I'd like you to confirm it. You were asked by my former colleague, Mrs. Korner: "You heard, didn't you, almost immediately that there had been a massacre of some 60-odd Muslims by members of the military and the police?" And your response was: "Yes, I heard about that, but I don't know how many people fell casualty." Can you confirm that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could just now go back to the document we had on the screen just before this P520. Oh, sorry, a new document, P520. It's an order for further operations in respect of this same incident from Dragan Samardzija and it's dated 9 July, 1992. And if we could just have a look at 2d in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, it says here, that: "The Sanica police platoon is to move along the Sanica-Jabukovac-Donji Biljani route and establish a check-point in the sector of the Donji Biljani school for processing suspicious persons. Extreme cases should be sent to the Kljuc SJB for further processing." Now, Mr. Vracar, what you said you were actually doing on the day after this incident in the Brdjanin case is that you were doing guard duty in front of the police station that day. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And not only were you doing guard duty in front of the police station, you remembered that prisoners were brought there for questioning; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Some people were brought in, but I don't know where from. Do you understand that? Because the territory of the municipality is quite large in geographical terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on the 11th of July, you were on guard duty in front of the police station, you saw prisoners brought there for questioning, and your evidence in the Brdjanin case was that you also heard those prisoners being beaten; right? You can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: You know what? There was one guard in the station, inside, and I was outside. I didn't know all of the insignia and so on. But later on, I found out in the Adamovic case - was that the name? - Mr. Dzafic's statement, so the guards in front -- I mean, I as a guard in front could not know at all what was going on inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no one asked you. The simple question was: Whether, like in the Brdjanin case, whether it's your testimony today that you heard those prisoners being beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what? There were beatings. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you hear? Did you hear the blows, or did you hear the persons, when beaten, perhaps using their voice, screaming, whatever. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard that some people moaning but you see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. That is an answer to the question. All the rest you said does go around the question rather than respond to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Vracar, the people, what you heard in the police station on the 11th of July were the people who were brought from Biljani on the bus, according to the order by Mr. Samardzija. You heard those people being beaten as they were questioned at the station, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: You see, I was outside standing guard, and I could not hear and see everything. Actually, I didn't see anything, but I heard what I heard as I said to the Presiding Judge a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just want go back to one area related to the 27th of May. Now, you made the point a couple of times that you were on medical leave after the 27th of May. You were on medical leave at the time of the Velagici massacre. Do you remember that? You just said that earlier today.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I assumed my duties on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you talked at paragraph 17 about the whereabouts of the Serb TO on the 27th of May, and you talked about that at temporary transcript page 9 today, you were simply on medical leave. You had no personal experience of their whereabouts; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't with that unit, but I know that it was out there for exercises because I was not a member of the TO. A TO unit was sent to the area of Cadjevica for military exercises, training, because some of my relatives and neighbourings went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that all the Serb military forces in Kljuc on that day were not in the municipality. They were sent for training at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what day?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at the witness's statement, D789, one more time, paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here you said talking about incidents on the 27th of May, as you did in the previous paragraphs, by the way, not accepting for a moment that you have the date right in paragraph 16, but here you said in paragraph 17 that during those combat actions by the -- as you describe it the Muslim army, the TO battalion of the legitimate municipality of Kljuc was not in the town but they were in Manjaca. So I want to know what are you saying? Are you saying there were no Serb military forces in and around Kljuc that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying military forces or police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question relates to military forces, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There weren't any military men there but the police were there of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another document. It's 65 ter number 03117. And it dates from 2 November 1993. It's a supplement to monograph of the 1st Krajina Corps, and it talks about the Kljuc Battalion. All right. We could go over to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I want you to have a look at the -- towards the bottom of page 3 in your language, Mr. Vracar, and it's the third full paragraph after the list of names. And in English, of course, the same. And, Mr. Vracar, that says that when the armed conflict in Kljuc began, the entire battalion, and it refers to the Kljuc Battalion was relocated outside Kljuc from where it was deployed to mop up the town and the surrounding settlements and the decision to assign this task to the battalion was issued on May 27th. And units were deployed to the village of Reizovici, Hadzici, and Pudin Han. And anti-tank platoon attacked from their positions in Brezcice. And then it goes down further and says: "The task of the companies was to disarm all the paramilitary formations in the direction of the attacks and to arrest members of these formations." And it continues on in English, but in your language we would have to go to the following page, I think, where it says: "The following day, the Kljuc battalion was deployed to carry out the same task in the area of the village of Pudin Han, Vukovo Selo, Humici, Plemence, Vrhovo, and Peci."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down by reading from a document, especially names of places.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it indicates that a mopping-up operation in two more villages, Kamicak and Vrhpolje ensued. Those are all mixed or predominantly Muslim areas I've just named, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: What is it that you wish to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was, first, that those locations I've just named are all mixed or predominantly Muslim areas, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this directly contradicts the evidence that you've just given that there was no military in Kljuc that day. The military was there, they had a task, and the task was to go and mop up non-Serb areas. That's what the document says; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object as [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can read the document. And if it's all that my colleague wants this witness to confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we see the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether the witness agrees that the document contradicts his evidence. That's the question. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is written in the document that the decision was made on the 27th of May to mop up the terrain. That is to say after what had happened in Krasulje. It is only then that the TO Staff decided on the mop-up operation. Do read this again. Only a decision was made and the mop-up occurred later on, on the 30th, the 31st of May. There is a difference of three to four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Nothing further about this document. And I'd like to have this document marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only if we can know what's the date of this document. Does the Prosecution have any idea when it was created?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Ms. Edgerton mentioned it's from -- no, perhaps I'm ... let's have a look. Ms. Edgerton, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honours. I did mention it and the date appears on the top left-hand corner of both versions, 2 November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was my recollection that Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that handwritten date or there is anything official?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because in English version -- yeah, it says handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says handwritten. The document in the date is in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea who wrote that on the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I have no personal idea who wrote it on the document. But reading the document which reports, for example, on the very last page on events at the end of August and September 1993, one is certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One recognises that the date is likely to be an accurate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, accurate or not, but at least it most likely is not any earlier than the last date mentioned in the document and the 2nd of November is later. Does this sufficiently clarify the questions you have? I think the parties would agree that on the basis of the content of the document, it was created considerably after the events described in 1992 because it also describes events in -- if you would agree, in August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3117 receives number P6932, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vracar, you also said in your statement, and I want to go back to that for a bit, in paragraph 4 that the victory of the SDS in Kljuc during the multi-party elections was followed by a split in the police force because Muslim police officers were refusing to wear Serb insignia. Now, you mean the multi-party elections in November 1990; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the refusal to wear Serb insignia that you referred to didn't happen until the MUP split in Kljuc on the 7th of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, it was then that the Muslims left the service because they didn't want to express their loyalty to the newly elected authorities, so most of them went on leave which was then followed by these incidents and the war broke out, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, sorry, when you talk about the newly elected authorities, you're talking about the authorities that were elected in November 1990, and in Kljuc, while the SDS won the elections, what was elected in November 1990 was a coalition. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Now, look, I didn't participate in those political games. I don't know who was in coalition with whom and probably they parted their ways at the end. Now why that was, that's a question for the politicians and their disagreement led to everything, on the entire territory and wider.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm a little bit puzzled by your question that was a coalition elected where the SDS had won the elections or did the SDS win the election and was then a coalition formed after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In an effort to speak efficiently, perhaps if I've caused confusion, Your Honour, but, in fact, the SDS won the elections but according to the decisions on the distribution of power. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see your point, but I was a bit confused by your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what -- Mr. Vracar, you talked about political gains but you've given evidence about the inter -- what Mr. Lukic described as the interethnic breakdown in society. You've given evidence about an increase in interethnic tensions in Kljuc. Now, in fact, that happened over the course of that whole year and a half you skipped over in your statement, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Madam, that's not a year and a half. This conflict had been going on for centuries. You understand? You cannot accomplish the two ethnicities or three, get on those quarrelling terms in a year and a half. No. This happened over centuries, you understand? The first great wear, the second great war, and then the last war. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: -- inherited. This is something inherited from history.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question isn't about history. My question is about the year and a half that preceded the split of the MUP. And I'll ask the question in a different way. Since you actually do seem to be following -- have been following politics, you would know that the Autonomous Region of the Krajina was proclaimed in September 1991. You must know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... too late but witness was talking about the history not about politics and the claim that since this witness was following politics and the question arose from that, but he exclusively said that did he not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, this is comment rather than any objection. Let's leave it to that. The comment is on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that the proclamation of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina didn't increase interethnic tensions in Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, of course it increased the interethnic tension among the non-Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, let's look at a document. Could we see 65 ter 06877, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also seek clarification. Witness, you said: "Well, of course it increased the interethnic tension among the non-Serb people." Would you say interethnic tension between those who were not Serbs, that would mean Croats and Muslims, or was it interethnic tension between Serbs and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was tension between Serbs and those who are non-Serbian; in other words, Muslims and Catholics. And this proceeded -- this incident was proceeded by a referendum in March -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to fully understand what you said, interethnic tension among non-Serbs. No, it was interethnic tension between Serbs and non-Serbs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here in front of you is a document dating 29 October, 1991, and that's when Mr. Brdjanin, whose trial you appeared at, circulated an order from the Sarajevo SDS which had been circulated or presented at a meeting between Dr. Karadzic and all the mayors, and accepted by the ARK presidency. And this document -- have a look at point number 1. This document that Mr. Brdjanin circulates says to the municipality authorities: Establish commands, set up duty round the clock. And then at point number 2 it says: Mobilise the TO. And at point number 3 it says: Form field units. And then if you go down to number 5 it says: Take over power -- take over management, pardon me, in public enterprises by all means. So are you saying that this didn't contribute to interethnic tensions in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the document should be read properly. Point 2 was not read. It says, "Establish full mobility ...," and it was presented it was mobilisation. So I don't think that's said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mobilise the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently you say the way in which it was read does not reflect the actual text of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you please -- of course, the Chamber could not prepare for this. But you see that there seems to be an issue about mobility or mobilisation. Could we -- and is it a translation issue, Mr. Lukic, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Edgerton, now you know what problem Mr. Lukic had. You relieve him from those problems and you put the question again to the witness and you refer to the document in such a way that even Mr. Lukic would not have any problems with it any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What I'll do is I'll read, again, the first five passages of the document, and I'd like to have you, Mr. Vracar, read aloud for us point number 2 when we get to it. In this instruction, Mr. Brdjanin says the following, point 1: "Immediately form a command of the town and set up round-the-clock duty." Could you now read point 2 for us, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It says: "Establish full mobility of the Territorial Defence." In other words, the full mobility of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not -- you're just invited to read not to further explain. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Point number 3: "Form units for the front and designate their replacements? Number 4 reads: "All men under the age of 40 to be reassigned from civilian protection to the Territorial Defence, and the Territorial Defence to be resubordinated to the corps as war-time units." And, finally, number 5: "Take over management in public enterprises, the post office, the SDK, the bank," and so forth. Now, I'll ask the same question. Are you saying that this didn't contribute to interethnic tension in Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer your question. This is a political document. I cannot analyse or figure out what kind of ramifications did -- this had and -- among the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what Ms. Edgerton apparently is seeking is the following: In your statement, you give a picture in which, after the 1990 elections, suddenly a problem arises caused by the Muslims in early 1992; whereas, Ms. Edgerton puts to you certain documents which shed a different light on what happened and, that is, that there was a development in which documents like the one shown to you may have contributed to interethnic tensions which came not or certainly not exclusively from the non-Serb side. Ms. Edgerton, is that what you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please comment on that rather than to tell us that this is a political document. It is. Could you explain why you gave a different picture compared to what is now shown to you on the basis of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document for sure contributed to interethnic tensions. That's correct. It did contribute to the tension among all the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So is that to say that your picture at least is incomplete about what caused tensions at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained a moment ago that I wasn't involved in politics. I only know fragments about certain thing -- of certain things. As for this topic, I'm no expert, really. It was just the things that I could hear or see as your regular citizen because politics is something that's really miraculous, in a way. And I'm not involved in politics. I wasn't then and I'm not to this -- and I am not today, and giving any assessment on my part would be, well, not serious enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. So you say you have only fragmented information. Do you have any explanation as to why the fragments you were familiar with are mainly favourable to the Serb side and unfavorable to the non-Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know how it is. You receive all kinds of information through the news. We received information via the media, TV, and so on. Now, on the basis of that information, well, my position is what it is. Some people like one thing, other people like another thing. It's a question of choice, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber is not interested in what kind of information you like but about the facts that occurred. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have that document as a Prosecution exhibit and then I'll change topics. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6877 receives number P6933, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said at paragraph 27 of your statement that the moving out of the civilians was not a policy of the RS or the VRS. So can I understand that, or can we understand that to mean that you're trying to say that the moving out of the non-Serb civilians from Kljuc was not a government or a military policy? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That was not a municipal policy or the government policy, to expel people by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that forcible expulsions -- no, actually, let's go back to the words you used. You said "moving out of the civilians." What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The war broke out, and then there was chaos. People were afraid --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Vracar, what did you mean to explain when you talked about moving out? Are you talking -- are you limiting your statement to forcible expulsions of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No. Voluntary moving out. They just were moving out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that that is not a policy. It wasn't a policy anywhere in the Autonomous Region of the Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me about the entire Krajina. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you should put this part of the statement of the witness on the screen again. And it's -- this sentence not referring to the Autonomous Region of Krajina but Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Could we have D789 on the screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vracar, you said in your statement it wasn't a government -- the moving out of civilians wasn't a government policy across the whole Republika Srpska. And you said it wasn't a military policy.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: It wasn't that policy. That's correct. It wasn't anyone's policy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So even to take that down from -- from the whole entity that you're talking about to the region you lived in, you're saying that that wasn't a policy anywhere in Kljuc, in Prijedor, in Sanski Most. The moving out of civilians wasn't a policy anywhere in the country and particularly in these locations. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That is not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, do you want to explain? Did they -- were people moved out as part of a state and military policy or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: People followed their armies. Muslims went one way; Serbs another way; and the Croats went the third way. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're mixing up at this moment what happened and what policy was. Now to link the events to the policy would be the next step but let's start with the beginning. Was there any -- a formulated policy by the Republika Srpska that non-Serbs would move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, there were some instructions - and we were told so - that people should not be compelled to leave, that they shouldn't leave. And this is then -- this was implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, in your statement, we do not find anything about that. But then could I ask you, people should not be compelled, should they be encourage, or should they be put in a position where it was -- hmm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Compelled, forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's no need to interrupt me at that moment. But were there any other means to be used to make them move out other than force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. These answers, are they true, both for government policy and for military policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any local policy which would be different? And we start with Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All local authorities had to implement the government decisions, the Republika Srpska government, and in that sense, there were instructions issued. The Defence counsel also showed me some documents, and I knew that also from our life, that there shouldn't be mistreatment and forcible moving out of people, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're again rephrasing the issue. My question is whether you were aware of any local policy which would be different from what you just described and we start with Kljuc. Was there, in Kljuc, ever any policy developed different from the one you described at the government level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other municipality where a different policy would have been adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be honest, believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In point of fact, Mr. Vracar, in every one of these municipalities that I named, including Kljuc, municipalities that had significant Muslim populations, the Serbian authorities took the decision that non-Serbs had to leave. And that's what's happened. And they took that decision as part of a policy. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I never saw any decision of that sort. That would be completely outside any normal thinking, you know, that anyone should take a decision like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at P3753.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a document dated 7 June, 1992, and it's a set of conclusions adopted at a subregional meeting of the political representatives of the municipalities of Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi and Kljuc. And if we can go down to paragraph 6 in this document. Paragraph 6 says that: "All seven municipalities in their subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities." And if you go back to the first page, you see that the conclusions from this meeting were sent to the ARK Crisis Staff and to the Bosnian Serb leadership in Sarajevo. So not only have your government authorities taken a decision like that in the subregion you lived in, you agree that this is a completely abnormal -- a decision that is completely outside any normal thinking; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand that Ms. Edgerton was not with us before, but you know that we objected to this document and we would like to be presented to the witness that there is no known source who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is it admitted or is it not admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If there's a decision, we don't have to make the witness familiar with whatever details. If the witness has any comments on it, the point, of course, is that the witness, from what I understand, at least, it's logically follows from his answers, that he was not familiar with this document, but we could ask him. Witness, have you ever seen this document before in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
