utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Unfortunately, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the witness could not assist us in any way. What Ms. Edgerton was doing, she was quoting from a document which is in evidence, and the authenticity of the document seems not to be within the purview of the knowledge of this witness. Therefore, Ms. Edgerton may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next time, Ms. Edgerton, if you say, next time, the decision as stated in this document, then you resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Understood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you pointed out in your written evidence, Mr. Vracar, that requests to move out of Kljuc municipality came after the attacks of the Muslims and Croats and it's at paragraph 27. We could display it in D789. To be exact, you said: "The requests to move out by the Muslims and Croats increased, in particular, after the military actions carried out by the Muslim and Croat forces." But, in fact, what exacerbated the situation and put fear into all of the non-Serb inhabitants of Kljuc was that after the attacks by the Muslim and Croat forces, Muslim and Croat settlements not only in Kljuc but across three municipalities were shelled, civilians were killed, and massive arrests of non-Serbs were taking place, arrests by the military and the police; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, after the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, as you said yourself, word of the massive killings in Velagici and Biljani were the talk of the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, let me -- your previous question gave a number of matters, and the witness said as an answer, "Yes, after the 27th of May..." Now I would like to remove any possible ambiguity. After the attacks by the Muslim and Croat forces, were -- civilians were killed in Muslim and Croat settlements? You agree that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That happened only after the 27th of May. On the 27th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm just seeking whether after the 27th of May this is what happened. Were Muslim and Croat settlements not only in Kljuc but across three municipalities, were they shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were massive arrests of non-Serbs taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to be sure that you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for me to be completely clear, who were these Muslim municipalities shelled by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] TO. The Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you are referring to what I think you earlier called the legitimate or the Serb TO. That's ... not any competing Muslim TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Oh, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if we have such a composite question which contains quite a few rather important elements then a simple yes, there's always a risk that a witness responds to what he heard last and that's what I tried to repair.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course and understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me clarify the last thing, were, after the 27th of May, also civilians, Muslim civilians, killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, for me. Sorry. There were sporadic cases. You see, there was a lot of gangs there, renegades, who were looting, torching killing. Of course, yes. It was very hard to introduce law and order in such a big area. With so few forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] the question was: Were civilians killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just answered that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we went through -- we heard earlier from you that it may have been men being killed also not by gangs of renegades. We went through that in quite some detail, isn't it, about what happened in Biljani, for example? So the killing of civilians was not exclusively committed by those gangs of renegades, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Earlier you said that you did know that they did it, but -- let's take a break. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just in respect of the Court's inquiry at the outset of the session, there is no objection to the extension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness leave the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you asked for an extension of time to respond to the 45th 92 bis motion. You asked for 30 days. That request is granted. The new deadline is now set for Monday, the 22nd of December, 2014. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, based on your request for time and your later correction, the Chamber wonders whether you would finish within the next session?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, that's actually why I was on my feet and I've been able to benefit from the reflection of the break, and I won't be having any further questions for the witness, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Lukic, how much time you think you would need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Half an hour, 40 minute, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we wait and see. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't expect the cross to finish this soon, so I didn't organise perfectly, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not your first day, Mr. Lukic, so -- but, we'll nevertheless try to extend the leniency to you as well. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Vracar, thank you very much. I won't have any further questions for you in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there will be more questions in re-examination by Mr. Lukic. So he will now start his re-examination. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have - and I -- give me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good day, Mr. Vracar.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you something about paragraph 8 of your statement in relation to the killing of Dusan Stojakovic. This is what I'd like to ask you: Did anyone open fire from your side at the Muslim army and their positions before they started firing at you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, we were the regular patrol, and we were driving by in a car, and they ambushed us. They fired at us, from an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You started saying something to us today. Page 18 of today's transcript, line 3, the question was -- let us look at paragraph 15 of your statement. And this is what you were asked: Did you not see the attack on the bus in which there were unarmed soldiers that attacked the Muslim forces? You confirmed that you had not seen that. And then you started out by saying: While I was in hospital, three dead persons were brought in and a few wounded persons. You didn't finish what it was that you had wanted to explain. Do you have anything to add to this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I was given medical aid there. They brought three dead soldiers in and three wounded soldiers. However, the three wounded persons, three wounded soldiers, succumbed to their wounds eventually and died.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the same page of today's transcript, you were asked about the attack at the repeater, and you said that you hadn't seen that personally, you confirmed that, did you see the consequences on the ground, the consequences of the destruction of that repeater?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, the citizens could no longer watch television because the repeater was on top of a hill that is dominant in that area. So once the repeater was destroyed, the entire area was under an information blockade, both in terms of radio and television. There was no signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all in the statement. The consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, still he had -- I wanted to show still he had some personal knowledge, not only that he heard about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But it's clear from the statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move on any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see P2538 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I hear 3528?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague just mentioned this document today during her examination, and the questions pertained to the killings in Velagici and paragraph 35 of your statement. This is a file cover. I would like to ask for page 7, please, in both versions. This is a criminal report that was submitted on the 5th of June, 1992, by an authorised officer of the military police. The persons against whom this criminal report was filed are listed there. We see eight persons in B/C/S, but in the English version we can see just one. However, the total is 12 persons who have been charged. I would like that ask for page 8 in B/C/S and page 10 in English, please. The reasons are mentioned. It says, "because." "Because" is the word that is used in English and in the original it is "sto je." In the second paragraph, we see a description of what happened on the 1st of June, 1992; that is to say, the criminal report was filed for something that happened four days before the report itself was filed. In the text, there is a description of what was found during those four days, in addition to the 12 perpetrators whose names and surnames are referred to. Since you are not aware of any details, I'm not going to torment you with any of that. The instructions that you received in the course of police work, did they say that crimes should be concealed or uncovered?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: The police dealt with all sorts of crimes that were committed: Beatings, lootings, killings, theft, all kinds of police work. I have been unaware of this document until now, and now I see this criminal report, and I actually know some of these persons or, rather, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand that you're unaware of this because this was done by the military police. We will be needing page 9 in B/C/S and page 11 in the English version. The last paragraph before the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to move to another -- to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see that a criminal report was filed against these persons for the crime of war crime against the civilian population. In the course of your work, were you in charge of uncovering crimes, you, personally, or were you just a member of the intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I was just a member of the intervention platoon. This was done by inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you kindly to focus on the conversations you had with the members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you done with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In this document, Witness, it is described that the task of the soldiers -- and perhaps we could have a look at page 10. Yes, it reads, under the "because": "The basic task of the unit was to gather civilians who were surrendering." Were you aware that civilians were either surrendering or were invited to surrender where you would usually expect soldiers to surrender, not civilians. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to explain when this incident occurred at Krasulje, then the units, the military units, came from the field. This document was shown, the order of Colonel Samardzija, to carry out a mop-up operation on a the ground and then these arrests occurred. So it was on the 29th or 30th. I cannot remember exactly. It was a long time ago. A Territorial Defence unit came from the area of Cadjevica, and they carried out a mop-up operation and arrests. I mean, I don't know who it was that was carrying out the arrests because I was not there, so I cannot give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is whether this sounds familiar to you, that you would invite civilians to surrender. Whereas, usually in war operation, you would leave the civilians alone and focus on soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably some of the persons who were arrested had been mobilised in the so-called Muslim armed forces. These people were interrogated, checked. That was the procedure. Of course, these people did not have uniforms in the classical sense. They were not an armed force in that way. Quite simply, this was a rebellion of Muslims. They had different weapons and different uniforms. This was a multi-coloured army. I don't know what the system of arrest was. I mean, that's a question that I do not know the answer to, I mean, what the guiding principle was for arresting people. Because in order to arrest someone, someone has to stand accused of something, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly my question. My question is, and I again put it to you, whether you are familiar with the system where civilians are gathered who have not surrendered. Talking about mobilised soldiers, you wouldn't call them civilians. Civilians are those who are not combatants, are not in the army, but are just out of that. Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to explain that system. I just know that we, as the civilian police, on orders, we brought in people who had done something wrong, who had stolen something, had torched property, looted, and so on. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put another question to the witness in -- with respect to this report. You said that - it's at the end of end of page 55: "I have been unaware of this document until now, and now I see this criminal report." In your statement, paragraph 35, you say: "I know with certainty that a report on this case was filed." Is that the same report, or was it another report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just heard that a report had been filed, that our investigation organs had filed a report. I mean, my people in the police told me that a report had been filed against the perpetrators. I hadn't seen this document. I didn't even know who the perpetrators of this crime were. I mean, I know some of them. Some of them were my neighbours and so on. It's not that I saw the document. I mean, I heard when I talked to people that a report, a criminal report, had been filed, but I was unaware of the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You now say you heard, "... when I talked to people." What kind of people did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, colleagues. Well, we're human beings, aren't we? And we talk about things, talk about everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your colleagues in the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Earlier you said you're unfamiliar with this report on the screen because it's from the military police. How do your colleagues know that a report by the military police was filed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would like me to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People talked about a report being filed, but it wasn't filed by the civilian -- civilian police. We're a small town. People talk about everything that happens. This is the third time I'm repeating this. I haven't seen the document itself. I didn't know who the perpetrators were, although I know some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why did you say in your statement: "I know with certainty that a report on this case was filed." While, at the same time, you are telling me that you heard it, that members of another unit wrote this report and you see it for the first time today. How could you have been certain about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll answer right now. It's very simple. For instance, at our police station, inspectors conducted various investigative actions. Now, if Inspector Gajic, for instance, tells me a report had been filed, there is absolutely no reason for me to doubt his words. He was -- I mean, as an unofficial public official. That's why I was certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Although the report was filed not by a colleague of yours; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I began asking you about these things. Do you know Mikajlo Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discusses with him, before you talked with me, about this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, Mikajlo and I know each other from the war period, and we're good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you had a conversation with him about this case before you talked about it with me?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the date, but that did occur once. That was a long time ago. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you talked about an interview, you weren't referring just to your conversation with me?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, with you, it was official. As with Mikajlo it was more a conversation. We're friends. We see each other from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how these questions are arising from the cross, and they're quite leading as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, they may not arise directly from cross, but I think I put a few questions to the witness before cross-examination which may have triggered some of these questions. Let me just have a look. One second, please. Yes, do I understand that Mr. Mitrovic is a personal friend of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a personal friend, that's a -- a term that is pretty broad. We are acquaintances, good acquaintances. He is a neighbour. You know, one person has few friend, but he is a good friend of mine. A neighbour, a good neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A good neighbour. Mr. Lukic, interviews are conducted by neighbours and friends?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic is a member of our team and he is on this statement, mentioned on this statement as somebody who took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's my question to you. So apparently if you're a member of the team, you just ignore that the investigator and the -- and the potential witness are friends and neighbours and you don't mention that and you just send that person to interview the potential witness. Is that how I have to understand the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I had hundred persons I would probably not do that but if I have only one investigator in the west of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would send him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's clear. That's -- that's your solution. And you wouldn't then, for full transparency, inform the Chamber that you were at a situation where you had no other choice then to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I informed this Chamber many times that we were understaffed, underpaid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's something for this Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're missing the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not missing the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're missing the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not missing the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about being --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I conducted the interview with this gentlemen myself and we are not friends. That's all I could do. I joined investigator the second time when we interviewed this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Preliminary conversation was done by only my investigator. Whenever you find that somebody spoke in 2013 with the witnesses and you find it on our statements, it's only investigator. Without me. Because in 2013 I was here on the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You apparently missed the point again, Mr. Lukic. I leave it to that. Think about it, what the point was I raised. My point was not whether you had trouble in finding someone to conduct or to have that conversation and whether you needed further resources. My problem is that apparently, without further explaining or without further consultation, that members of your team are, if even preliminary conversations with persons that are friends of them and are their neighbours, without transparently making that knowledge available to everyone in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, I have to state that this is the first time that I heard that Mikajlo Mitrovic is a friend of this gentleman. Then I would have to inquire about every single witness he talked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I leave it to that for the time being. Then your team members perhaps should have informed you about it. I am not saying that you -- I personally express any blame for you but then apparently your team members do not have the professional skills to inform lead counsel of a personal relationship they have with persons they're supposed to interview. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I have P6932 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vracar, you were shown this document entitled: Supplement to the monograph -- or for the monograph of the 1st Krajina Corps. And the date, 2nd November, 1993, is handwritten. And then under on the right-hand side, it says 93. A supplement for a monograph, have you -- did you ever see anything like that as an official document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, this is the first time that I see this. And also this is the first time that I hear that something like this was done during the war. That really doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, this is the first time that I see it. I'd never even heard about something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now be shown P6933, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was shown to you. It's an order from the SDS in Sarajevo, where it says that it was made public at a meeting of all municipal presidents on the 26th of October, 1991. And under 1, it says, "Immediately establish a command of the town ..." Are you -- do you know whether there was a Town Command in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, there was only the Secretariat of Territorial Defence. That was a municipal organ. It's not a command of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time did the SDS command with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No. The JNA was a state army. I mean, what do you mean a party commanding the army? That's -- that couldn't be. A party couldn't command the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the field, did you ever see that the -- the SDS commanding the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, Territorial Defence was still under the command of secretariats of the Territorial Defence of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, had management been -- been taken over as it says here: "Take over management in public enterprises, post office, bank, judiciary, the media." For instance, in your municipality, what was the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, each municipality had their own -- had their own management. What do you mean taking over management? There were people who worked there. There were directors, there were people who managed, managers. What do you mean take over authority? If someone was a director of an enterprise, he was a director. He couldn't just be fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Lukic, I understood the questions by Ms. Edgerton on this document to point at what may have been policy that was developed. I did not understand it as evidence that it -- this is what then finally happened. There may be other evidence about that, but that's how I understood Ms. Edgerton introduced the document. Is that correct, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the matter of whether this finally happened was not touched upon in cross-examination. It was mainly to test the evidence of the witness that never such policies were formulated or adopted. Therefore, could you please keep this in mind when you are re-examining on matters triggered by the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, did anyone ever present any of these items here as a policy that was to be implemented on the ground in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked whether a document of this nature could cause unrest among people of another ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, I went -- if something like this did happen, it would really be surprising. This is a political party document, not official authorities. Parties say all sorts of things. That's their problem. To me, this looks like propaganda of a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in part, you've already answered my next question now. Do you know whether this document was ever published anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it wasn't. This is the first time that I see a document of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about paragraph 27 of your statement and about the moving out of the population, and I will ask you this: Did you ever receive an order or instructions as a policeman or as a civilian to forcibly expelling anyone from your town?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, never. That was not the practice, and I can say that some 200 Serb families left. They left voluntarily. They fled the war. I couldn't go anywhere because my parents were bedridden. They were ill. There was nowhere I could go. I couldn't leave my own country. However, people were afraid. War is a great evil. And now when you don't have normal authorities that can actually maintain order on the entire territory, then -- when you can expect people to perhaps, you know, knock on your door in the middle of the night or torch your house. People were afraid. So people left on their own because it wasn't always possible to maintain law and order. There were 300 or 400 policemen for a territory that was about 800 square kilometres. That's not a small area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see -- even if you didn't get such an order or instructions, did you hear from a colleague that that colleague was ordered to persecute civilians?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, I don't know of such a case, that anyone ever ordered anyone to gather their family, to pack their stuff and leave, no, I never heard of anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P3753, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a document before us where -- in the heading, can you see which organ issued this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can also see that there is no number for this document. We see the date, 7 June, 1992. And this document says that these are conclusions adopted at a subregional meeting and then: "(Of political representatives of the following municipalities: Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi and Kljuc...)." In the course of your work, did you ever come across something called subregional -- subregion that would encompass these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I heard of this. What kind of subregion? It was an autonomous region or Autonomous Province of Krajina. This was someone fooling around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this time, on 7th of June, 1992, was Bihac under the control of Serb or Muslim forces? That's the first town mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Bihac was under the control of the BH army 5th Corps at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, our army never entered Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Did you ever receive a document or see a document that would come from a subregion, as is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next page in both versions. This is a paragraph that was put to you by my colleague the Prosecutor. It says that: "All seven municipalities in our subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities ..." Did you know at the time when the war started that political communities were established of municipalities that were under the control of the Muslim forces, like Bihac, and partly Serb municipalities, like the other six mentioned municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I didn't know that such political organisations were being developed at municipal level. This is the first time I see this. What kind of political community of the municipalities is this? Nothing. Who felt like anything like that at the time. There was a war going on and then somebody trying to invent some kind of associations. I mean, somebody just invented this. This never existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whether it existed or not, you have no knowledge about it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No. Thank God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then refrain from saying, I mean, somebody just invented this. This never existed. Because you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, you do not know of the existence of this subregion.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Correct. This is the first time I hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in conclusion, I'd just like to ask you something else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness clearly stated and by your last question, you ask him to contradict himself and you apparently accept that. The witness said, "This never existed."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that he has knowledge about the existence; namely, that it did not exist. That's what he claimed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when I said, So you don't know anything it, then you had a follow-up question that he -- that he did not know of the existence, whether that's correct -- okay. I leave it to that at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was follow-up question on your question, Your Honour, on page 68, line 21, when you proposed that this witness have no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to see if he has no knowledge at all or he does not know about the existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the same for me. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were also asked whether civilian settlements had been shelled. Do you know whether civilians were shelled, or military formations of the other side that were in civilian settlements?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Military formations were shelled, those that had positions in villages. Now, whether there were civilians there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to give a few clear examples. Could you give us the name of a settlement? Could you tell us what -- whether that settlement was shelled, when, and what target was then engaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the answer to that question. There are many details involved. I was not involved in these events, but there was shelling, that's for sure. When the terrain was mopped up, there was certainly fighting between the Muslims and the Serbs. And then there was firing from anything that people had. They fired at Serbs, and Serbs fired at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your explanation, you more or less deny your previous answer. May I take it that you have no knowledge about what targets specifically were engaged in those settlements, not being able to give any example of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not able.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then your previous answer was inaccurate, and you should not have given it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also asked about mass arrests. What is your knowledge about these mass arrests? What does it have to do with? Why was it the people were arrested en masse?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim side was called upon to surrender their weapons, and then people were bringing in these weapons. And then people were being interrogated, arrested, and so on. Probably on account of having had these weapons and also for armed rebellion. Because that's how it was taken. Armed rebellion against the legal authorities of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vracar. That's all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything about the return of Serbs and non-Serbs after the hostilities had taken an end?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mean after the war? To tell you quite frankly, about 20 persons returned to Kljuc; from 20.000 Serbs, that is. And when Muslims took over Kljuc, then all the Muslims returned to Kljuc. The Serbs moved to a variety of places, from Republika Srpska, Serbia, to America. Unfortunately, there are no Serbs left there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the 20, I do understand?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the Serb houses that were -- were they occupied later by Muslims or -- if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: For the most part, Serbs sold their houses at a very cheap price, at that; for example, 100 euro per square metre of housing. That is a ridiculous low price. It is basically seizure of property. Quite simply people did not have any living conditions there because there is no point in going back if you haven't got a job, you see, and if you do not receive a salary for a month, for another month, for a year, what can you live on? And nobody will give you employment there, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in the agricultural sector, would people, if they had a plot of land, would they -- in the agricultural sector, if people would have a plot of land, they did not return?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA VRACAR
utterances.text: I have to inform you of the following: The municipality of Kljuc was divided into two municipalities, the urban part came to belong to the Muslims, the north-west, the villages where they were majority to, those villages that gravitate towards town. The other part where I was born, Ribnik, that belongs to Republika Srpska and most of the people there are involved in agriculture and finishing, then about 700 people -- 7.000 people returned there and are involved in agriculture. They have livestock, et cetera, but they did not go back into town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. This concludes your testimony in this court, since I do understand that the parties have no further questions for you. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, it's a long way, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you and I wish you a safe return home again. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to thank you and the entire staff of this court. If my statements were of any use and if they will contribute to unraveling this entanglement, I will be gratified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we -- we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking at an audible level, Mr. Mladic. No speaking at an audible level, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, would you please now stop talking. Good morning, Mr. -- good afternoon, Mr. Barasin. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Barasin. Mr. Barasin, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic as you most probably know is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Barasin.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us for the record your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: My name is Ostoja Barasin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barasin, did you give a statement to members of the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D1660 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see a document before you on the screen. Can you see that signature?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes, and that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The information recorded in your statement, were they recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we see in your statement, is that true?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by every word that's written there. It's all true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender Mr. Barasin's statement into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1660 receives number D790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would just read statement summary of Mr. Barasin and then I will have only one question for him after that. May I? Thank you. Upon the formation of the 1st Krajina Corps, Mr. Barasin, Ostoja, joined the information office. The task of the office was to inform the public about the events in the AO replenishment, or area of -- of operation replenishment of the corps. The office organised the reception of local and international journalists and took them to the theatre of operations. The office hosted BBC, SkyNews, Paris Match. The journalist, Mehmed Dizdar, a Muslim, and contributor, Anton Kasipovic, a Croat, worked at the press centre from the beginning until the end. Mr. Barasin directed several documentaries, such as "Ratlines" and "Genocide Again." The documentary "Ratlines" is about a group of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia named Berbir who crossed the Sava river in Gradiska area in August 1992 in order to make a beachhead for the military operations in the Republika Srpska. A documentary, "Genocide Again" is about an atrocities committed by the Muslim-Croatian forces in Kupres, Brod, Derventa, village Serdari, et cetera, in 1992. The movie also features several witnesses depicting crimes. From 1993 until the end of 1995, Mr. Barasin was Chief of Staff and commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade and the 14th Light Infantry Brigade. As commander, he always took care of prisoners of war, and they were always treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. He did not allow either physical or mental abuse of prisoners. That was the short -- the statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you spoke about "Ratlines," is that the same as what we find in the statement as "Red Canals"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Red Canals," "Ratlines," yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- yes. If you have -- you said you had one more question. Please put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One question. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Barasin, these two video-clips that you provided to the Defence and we tendered, in some of those videos we see also presenters speaking, not just witnesses. Whose text is that, their words?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: The text read by the narrator, that's my text, and it's based on the various documents that I received from the security and intelligence organ, but also from civilian sources. So not only military but also civilian sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would now tender six documents, six associated exhibits with Mr. Barasin's statement, including two video-clips, but we would like to say at this point that we will only rely on the transcribed versions of the video. In other words, the portions of the video-clip that have transcripts attached to them. But we would also like to rely on the words of the narrators, as well as those of the interviewed witnesses. We came up to six exhibits because we had to actually divvy up two transcripts into four different transcripts because there was a confusion about the order in which they follow. So, at this point, we would normally have wanted to tender four documents but we will actually tender six exhibits, which, in fact, boils down to two video-clips with their accompanying transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We have no objection to any of the exhibits. I understand that Mr. Lukic is relying on only the -- the portions of the videos for which this are transcripts, only relying on the narrators' speech when it is transcribed. We spoke about this today, and we reserve the right to tender additional portions for context, but we have no objection to proceeding as Mr. Lukic has suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Madam Registrar, the first one, 02924, would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Then 05992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Then the first portion of the "Red Channels", part 1, 1D06005.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D793, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Then same number, with a small a added to it, being the second part of "Rat Channels."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Part 1 of "Genocide Again," being number 1D06004.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same number, with a small a added being part 2 of "Genocide Again".

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D796, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are also -- both of them are admitted. I see that the title is here "Genocide Again" whereas, in the statement it's "Genocide All Over Again," but I take it that that's all the same. You have no further questions, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to -- to cross-examine the witness, I would have one question for you. These videos you -- you created, was it your purpose to specifically focus on the suffering of the Serb -- of the Serbs, or was it your intention to give an overall view of the suffering of people of all ethnicities during the war? Or was -- did you have another objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my only objective in "Genocide Again" was exclusively to document the suffering of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the other video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other video dealt with a specific incident. It deals -- the "Ratlines" deals with a war-time incident in Kotor Varos when a group of Muslims, infiltrating a territory that had not been at war yet, tried to urge the Muslim population to rebellion, and this film, as mentioned before, has to do with Gradiska and Berbir. These two events are related because the incursion into Gradiska in August 1991, the objective of that incursion was to move against Banja Luka from the territory of Croatia, whereas "Ratlines" had to do with actually fermenting rebellion among the Muslim population --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part. It is due to your speed of speech that parts of your answer is missing. Could you please repeat the last part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. The Gradiska events in August 1992 are related to the film "Ratlines" that was produced in early July 1993. They're linked because the incursion of the Muslim Croatian forces from Croatia into the northern part of Bosnia had as their objective an attack on Banja Luka and the capturing of that part of Republika Srpska, whereas the "Ratlines" incident has -- was in Kotor Varos. A group of Muslim soldiers infiltrated Kotor Varos or, rather, Siprage and Kovacevici village with the intention of fermenting among the population, the Muslim population that lived there and that did not take part in the fighting, to ferment rebellion so that, then, they could attack Kotor Varos, Celinac and continue their operations towards Banja Luka. From a military perspective --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But from what I understand, is that your videos were focusing on operations activities, whatever, directed against the Serbs by the Muslims and do not pretend to give an overall view of what happened in the conflict areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to make it abundantly clear, these videos were your creation. They are not the recording of what took place on the ground. They are entirely your creation. I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I created them but within the context of the events that are discussed -- shown there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll first introduce you to the witness. Mr. Barasin, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find him to your right, and Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, today, in fact, just now, at temporary transcript page 79, lines 12 through 14, you testified: "My only objective in 'Genocide Again' was exclusively to document the suffering of the Serbian people." You made this documentary in the course of your service in the organ for legal, morale and religious affairs of the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who provided you with that objective for your work?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Well, I proposed this, the production of this video, and I did it at my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To whom would you have had to propose it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: I proposed it to the chief of the organ for morale, the corps organ for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was your superior officer; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At that time, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Colonel Milutin Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 4 of your statement that from 1991 until the establishment of the VRS, you worked at the JNA 5th Corps press centre. As of the beginning of May 1992, who was your superior officer in the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Colonel Milutin Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was there not a point when the head of the organ for moral guidance in the 5th Corps was Mesud Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: He was there briefly, but I didn't work with him. But I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say he was there briefly. He was there in the 5th Corps but stopped being present around the time that the 5th Corps was transformed in the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Colonel Hasotic was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, where were you yourself based as an officer in the organ for legal, morale and religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: At the time, it was the JNA club. Today, it is the municipal -- the Assembly of Banja Luka. So it's in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is in Banja Luka. When the 5th Corps was transformed into the 1st Krajina Corps, did you continue to be based in the same office?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were you, during the period of 1992 up till July 1993 when you joined the 5th Kozara Brigade, were you out in the field on the front lines during combat, or were you based in Banja Luka in that office?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: No, I was in the field but in various areas depending on our planned activities. I was in all those positions which were in the area of responsibility of the 5th originally and then later on the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the purpose of the organ for legal, morale and religious affairs, among other things, is monitoring, analysing, planning and organising moral education in the subordinate units; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, in simple terms, that means part of your job is telling the soldiers what they're fighting for; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: That was not my job. My job was informing the general public on the developments on the front lines, the areas where combat was ongoing. There were other people within the morale organ who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I spoke imprecisely, I think, sir, but you've clarified any ambiguity, and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we look briefly at Exhibit P2874.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this document is dated the 21st of May, 1992, and it's coming from Colonel Vukelic, your superior. And it reports here on page 1 of the English and B/C/S in the second sentence that a major transformation of the army has taken place. Turning to page 2 of the English and at the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S, the document reads: "The constituent Serbian people, who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of BH, must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples and form their own state." And if we turn to the end of the document in both languages -- I apologise. The end of the text so the previous page in the B/C/S. We read: "Inform all members of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH about the contents of this report in the most suitable way." So this is part of what we just discussed, the organ for legal, morale and religious affairs telling the soldiers what they're fighting for; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The organ for legal, morale and religious affairs wouldn't set those political goals themselves. From whom would they receive them, or information as to the political goals of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Well, every army, including that of Republika Srpska, has a chain of command, so the corps command received their orders from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, whereas, the Main Staff received their orders from the main command. Command in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so the purposes -- what the soldiers were fighting for, would you disseminated down from the Main Staff to the corps through the organ for legal, morale and religious affairs to the soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Inter alia, that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the 1st Krajina Corps press centre - and I'm done with this document, Your Honours - published a magazine called "Krajiski Vojnik" during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who was in charge of determining the content of that magazine?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Well, there was an editorial board, and certainly it was the editors that prepared that periodical, and together with the chief for morale it was reviewed in the final version, and that's when we had it printed. On the other hand, the content of the periodical reflected the current situation at combat positions and, in that way, we made sure that our soldiers were informed about what was going on, both at the front line and on the political scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was "Krajiski Vojnik" distributed then to units within the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 11820 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, you mentioned a moment ago that the chief for legal, morale and religious affairs would review the content of the periodical with the editorial board. Were the members of the editorial board also soldiers in that organ?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: Not only military personnel. We had journalists who worked there too. And a number of journalists had been mobilised, actually, into the Army of Republika Srpska. Other journalists volunteered to work there. They were not under any kind of obligation. So they wrote as freelance contributors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is one article that was published in "Krajiski Vojnik" in the fall of 1993. I'm looking for page 3 in the English and the third column on the left side, the second full paragraph, in the B/C/S. And this is portions of a speech by President Karadzic to the VRS officers' school. And I'm looking for the third column in the -- so ... yeah. I'm obliged. Now, President Karadzic is speaking. And he says: "The Republic of Serb Krajina shares our fate and we, when we speak of ourselves, do not set that apart, because we speak of people as a whole. I would already tomorrow consent to unification with Serbia. Not into a federation but into a unitary state, with districts as Serbia has?" And he continues. But at the end of the paragraph, he says: "For Serbs, there is only one capital: Belgrade." So my question for you is just: It's correct, isn't it, that "Krajiski Vojnik" published articles arguing that all Serbs should live in one state?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA BARASIN
utterances.text: First of all, President Karadzic at that time was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces and I, as a soldier at that time - and today - I cannot comment upon what the Supreme Commander says. A soldier is a soldier. Secondly, I wish to say that what he said has to be viewed in a broader historical context and, of course, I wouldn't have the time to explain all of that now. What happened to the Serb people -- and also what happened has a broader historical context and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, you're saying that you cannot comment on what President Karadzic said. You were not invited to do so. The simple question was whether you agree that the "Krajiski Vojnik" published articles in which it was argued that all Serbs should live in one state. And I think that Mr. Traldi used this as a specific example of such a publication. Do you agree that that is the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Krajiski Vojnik" published an interview with President Karadzic. So it was not the views of the editors that were reflected here. It was the interviewee himself, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not asked that question, but you do agree that in this interview that we find that -- and which was published, that we find an opinion expressed which argued that all Serbs should live in one state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that that is written here, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 11820. And I think I may suggest that I not proceed for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's a good suggestion. Let's first ask Madam Registrar for a number for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11820 receives number P6934, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Barasin, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back, not tomorrow because we're not sitting but Monday, the 24th of November, 9.30 in the morning. But before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with anyone, whomever, including Defence, Prosecution, no one, you should not communicate with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony still -- given or still to be given. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to interrupt. We have fixed videolink in the morning. And I cannot contact this witness anymore, so just to inform him that it will not be 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then that videolink is scheduled for how long; do you know? Half an hour for chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think our cross estimate was one and a half, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One and a half. Two hours in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to you to make yourself available during the second half of the morning. We cannot assure you that we are ready then to re-start your examination. But you don't have to be here at 9.30. If that is all clear to you -- And thank you, Mr. [Overlapping speakers] ... Then you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic, I had lost that totally out of my mind which should not have happened, but ... We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume, Monday, the 24th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
